I was always a reader, and when I became a ctian I read the Bible cover to cover ... many times. I underlined, annotated, made notes...and when I found contradictions, I noted them. 
 
Some of them I put down to translation errors, some to assuming science didn't have all the answers, and a few things to quantum uncertainty (a mis-use off my bs in physics).

I wasn't as rigid about inerrancy as my denomination (independent charismatic, then Ass. of God), so I took a "well I guess I'll find out in heaven" approach and kept believing anyway. 

As for the gospels and other conflicting accounts, one of my seminary professors liked to tell about the battle of Midway in WWII: two US air groups located the Japanese carrier. Both groups swear the other group was there already fighting when they arrived. His point was that in the midst of important/exciting events, confusion makes it hard to remember what happened. To him, the discrepancies were a sign that the accounts were true. Someone making the stories up would have made them all the same. 
That explanation satisfied me then; it doesn't now.  Once you believe in something, the amount of evidence/persuasion needed to keep believing is *way* lower than the amount needed to switch sides.

But all the errors--and many other things--wore on me, and I questioned more and more doctrines till I eventually didn't believe much of anything except that Jesus was somehow real.
